articles.title: Julian Macdonald among fashion designers keen to put Wales on industry map
articles.summary: Creatives say they can thrive in the fashion industry without having to move to a big city.
articles.body:
Do you need to go to a big city to work in fashion?

Former director at Givenchy, Julien Macdonald doesn't think so, nor does Ioan Bowen-Pickett, a young Welsh fashion designer.

Macdonald said there was no need for aspiring designers to leave for cities such London any more, thanks to a device you're likely reading this article on.

When Fashion Britain, a concept born by the British Fashion Council (BFC) originally launched its scheme to take fashion on a tour of the UK beyond London, it had excluded Wales.

But after campaigning by industry figures the BFC reversed its decision, with many saying the events that happened as a result were vital to championing Wales.

Macdonald, who was awarded an OBE in 2006, has worked for Chanel and Givenchy as well as establishing his own clothing brand, and stars including Beyonce, Taylor Swift and Suki Waterhouse have all worn his clothes.

But he said the fashion industry now is radically different from 35 years ago when the teenage boy with a love of knitting and art had to leave Merthyr Tydfil for Brighton, then London, before his talent was spotted by the fashion icon Karl Lagerfeld.

"Gone are the days that you needed to be in a city because now you've all got something that's right in your hands or by the side of you.

"It's called a phone. You can create a brand, a virtual shop on a phone and you can create your own business in Wales. If it's made in Wales it's even better.

"Now everybody has access to fashion. It doesn't matter whether you're in the valleys, in Cardiff City, at the top of a mountain, fashion is for everybody just by the touch of a button."

Macdonald was speaking on a Fashion Britain panel in Cardiff featuring high-profile Welsh industry figures including designer Jayne Pierson , creative director Charlotte James and Ibby Abdi , who's collaborated with New Balance and Cardiff City.

He said events like this were "just the start of things to come".

But when the BFC first launched its high-profile Fashion Britain campaign to encourage the industry to look at the range of British talent working outside London, it announced events in cities such as Bristol, Manchester, Dundee and Edinburgh.

When there was no mention of Wales designers such as Ioan Bowen-Pickett took to social media to express their disappointment.

Bowen-Pickett, 25, has his own fashion brand Cambrensis, based in Cardiff, placing Wales' rich cultural and industrial heritage front and centre in his high-end designs.

He's already announced a collaboration with Clarks Shoes and hosted pop-up stores at branches of John Lewis.

The designer says he can "100%" do it without moving to London.

He said: "What's the point? It's too crowded in London, there's too much noise."

"There's a massive opportunity in doing what we're doing in Wales currently. It's an unbelievably talented set of people in this country."

When the BFC's chief executive re-shared Ioan's video on Instagram, it signalled the announcement of a dozen or so events introduced across Wales.

Cambrensis hosted its own event, with a launch for a promotional video and brand ambassador, Alex Vlhaos, in a bar in Cardiff.

The event was sold out, with guests from the fashion industry in south Wales invited to network, and celebrate the work they do.

Jade Matthews and Morgan Mcloughlin attended the event, which Morgan said was "important" for Welsh culture and designers from Wales.

"It's exciting, we're being seen, we're being put on the map," Matthews added.

Amy Jenkins, a self-employed hair and make-up artist from Pontypridd, said: "We sometimes are overlooked, overshadowed and from personal experience it's difficult to get out there sometimes."

Jenkins works with actress Emma Myers, known for the series Wednesday and the Minecraft movie.

"I do her hair and makeup for the occasional events and I worked as her hair and makeup artist on Good Girls Guide to Murder," Jenkins added.

"I go pretty much wherever I'm asked to go, I did a press tour last year and I got to go to South Korea and Australia."

'We don't want it to be a one-off moment'

Natalie Potter from the BFC said: "London is the global fashion capital, but British fashion has never been created in one place.

"We have to make sure opportunity, visibility and investment reach beyond London.

"And that means going into communities, meeting people where they are and creating opportunities for audiences to engage with fashion on their very own doorstep."

Potter said she did not want this to be a "one-off" moment.

"We want to build relationships with cities and communities across Britain and create more opportunities for designers, maker businesses and audiences outside of London," she said.

Some will argue that not everything can be achieved here in Wales and some will have to make the move in order to get experience.

Naomi Pike, commissioning editor at Elle UK, moved to London from Swansea to pursue a career in fashion.

She said it was "really exciting" that events like Fashion Britain were being expanded outside of London.

"I know when I was growing up, I would have been supremely excited to go to something such as this," she said.

Pike, who hosted various events in collaboration with Elle and Fashion Britain, spoke about the importance of community and networking at events like this.

"Finding people that have like-minded views, shared values, and you can build and support each other," she said.

"I think there is a place for fashion in Wales, there's a long way for it to go to compete with anything that we see in the other big capitals.

"But Wales, for instance, has always had its place in fashion. There have been so many designers that have referenced our amazing craft and heritage.

"I think of Sarah Burton when she was at Alexander McQueen. She often looked to our craft. You see people like Jonathan Anderson and Phoebe Filo, two of the world's most important designers, look to Gwyn John for art inspiration."

Pike said Welshness can be a unique selling point.

"Welsh creativity, I think is very singular. The existence of being Welsh, whether you're in London, whether you're in another part of Britain, whether you're in another part of the world is very singular.

articles.summary: The teacher killed in a shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shooting was identified by police on Friday as 25-year-old Meghan, Lambert. The hero who took down the shooter was Kaylub Giamanco.
articles.body: The man who police in Bend, Oregon, said "neutralized" the 16-year-old shooter who killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School has been identified as 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, a law enforcement source confirmed to Fox News Digital. During a news conference Friday, police identified the teacher who was killed in the shooting as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert, and also announced that among the youngest of the victims was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. "Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. Her friends became her family," Lambert's family said in a statement read at the news conference. ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS "Yesterday was a terrible day for our community," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during the news conference. "Five people succumbed to their injuries at the scene, including the suspect. "The deceased at the school scene included three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one 25-year-old teacher. One 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported by Bend Fire to Saint Charles Bend with critical injuries." The 7-year-old is in serious but stable condition, and the 54-year-old teacher suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Krantz said that at 12:58 p.m. a witness who was driving by the school saw the suspect throw his gun over a fence and then climb the fence onto school property. He said the witness confronted the suspect who then fired at his truck, hitting it at least three times. The driver, who was not injured by the gunfire, went down the street and made the initial 911 call at 12:59 p.m., he said. Giamanco, who Krantz only identified as a "36-year-old man" during the briefing, drove into the school parking lot after seeing the suspect shoot at the truck, Krantz said, and saw the suspect shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside. POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING Once he was inside, the shooter went straight into the classroom that was to the left and fired as many as 15 rounds. Krantz said the shooter used three types of ammunition and that all the victims were shot in the classroom. Giamanco grabbed a .40-caliber pistol he legally kept in his car and went into the school through the same doors. After hearing the sounds of a shooting, he went into the classroom where he saw the suspect struggling with a teacher, who had tackled the shooter. Giamanco shot him multiple times. "In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize," Krantz said. "A teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect, and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. "She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed." DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED Police arrived at the school within minutes of the 911 call at 1:02 p.m. having been told that the "suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him, shooting him several times," Krantz said. Earlier Friday, Kenda Freeman said in a statement that her son, Giamanco, intervened in the attack and shot the gunman who killed three students and a teacher, The Associated Press reported. Giamanco, a local carpenter and dad, has two daughters who attend Silver Rail, his brother Kyle Gianmaco told NBC News. Kyle shared that Kaylub is shaken by the event and doesn't want to speak to the public. "We want the bystander who intervened to know we know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful, and we think he is a hero," Lambert's family added in the statement. "You selflessly put yourself at risk for others. We would like the other families to know they are in our thoughts and prayers. Megan loved those children, and so we will show you love for her." Tina Kotek praised school staff, parents and first responders, along with the community member "who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." articles.title: Oregon school shooting: 16-yr-old who killed 4 used mother's gun, targeted special needs class
articles.summary: A 16-year-old former student opened fire inside a special needs classroom at an elementary school in Oregon, killing three children and a teacher, after
articles.body: A 16-year-old former student opened fire inside a special needs classroom at an elementary school in Oregon, killing three children and a teacher, after allegedly forcing his way into the building with a shotgun bought by his mother, according to police and media reports. The attacker, identified as Griffin J. John II, was eventually stopped by a father who followed him into the school and shot him.The shooting took place at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend on Thursday. The victims were three children aged five, eight and 11, and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. A seven-year-old child who uses a wheelchair and a 54-year-old teacher were also injured in the attack, according to The New York Post.Police said all four fatalities occurred in the same classroom, which John had previously attended as a special needs student. Authorities said the teenager fired as many as 15 rounds from a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun. He reportedly had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed. Investigators are still examining the motive behind the attack and how the teenager obtained the firearm.Teacher tackled gunman as father intervenedAccording to The New York Post, citing law-enforcement sources, John threw his Maverick 88 shotgun over a fence at the school around 1pm on Thursday before climbing over it himself. He initially attempted to enter through the front door but was stopped by two bystanders, including a father of two pupils who had noticed the breach while driving past on his way home for lunch.The father, who was carrying a concealed firearm, opened fire on the teenager, disrupting his attempt to enter through the front. John then allegedly ran around to the rear of the building, forced open a locked door and made his way to his former classroom, where he opened fire.Police Chief Mike Krantz said a teacher confronted the gunman by throwing her phone at him before tackling and fighting him in an attempt to seize his weapon. She was not injured.Krantz praised her actions during a news conference, describing her as someone who was willing to stand and fight for her pupils. He also credited the father who shot the attacker, saying the two intervened to stop the violence and save lives.School district official Steve Cook said the school would investigate its emergency response procedures following the shooting. He added that students practised lockdown drills twice a year and that the latest drill had taken place about two weeks earlier.Shooter's mother expresses griefJohn's mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that she was devastated by the attack. According to The New York Times and CNN, she broke down while speaking about her son and the victims.“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said. “I'm so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I'm sorry for their loss.”She also described her son as a “good boy”, according to The New York Post. The newspaper, citing law-enforcement sources, reported that Nickerson had legally purchased the shotgun around the time of her son's birthday in August.Police have not established why John targeted the classroom or what led him to carry out the attack. Krantz said investigators were seeking answers but cautioned that the full explanation might never emerge.“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” the police chief said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”Lambert's family remembered the 25-year-old teacher as compassionate and devoted to children. Police communications manager Sheila Miller said teaching at Silver Rail Elementary had been Lambert's first job and that working in the school district she loved had been her dream.You use AI every day. articles.title: Teacher tackled and fought Oregon school shooter
articles.summary: By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult...
articles.body:
BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said on Friday.

A day ‌into their investigation of the latest U.S. school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail ‌Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, ​but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.

"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.

As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.

Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school, upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter ‌was dead, police said.

In the meantime the 16-year-old assailant, who ⁠had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.

Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, "I don't think we can underestimate ⁠or under-appreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that."

He said that the bystander's actions "undoubtedly saved people," and "the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism."

Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom ​and ​had another 44 rounds on him.

The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother ​told the New York Times. She identified him as the ‌father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said. "Kaylub's family, including his two daughters who attend the school, respectfully asks for privacy during this difficult time, and will not be participating in interviews at this time."

Residents of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles just outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the ‌scene.

"Thank God for that father. He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should ​go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today. We wish him well, ​and thank God for him," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks ​from the school, said through tears.

Brooke Olsen, the mother of a kindergartener who was safely reunited with her family after the shooting, ‌also expressed gratitude for the man who stopped the shooter.

"This is ​an extremely painful day of grief for ​everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families, and we have to think about what's next for safety measures."

Such school shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debates over gun laws in a country where a right to "keep and bear Arms" is protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment.

Some ​of the deadliest school attacks in the US include those ‌at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018 and Robb Elementary School in ​Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.

(Reporting by Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom in Bend; Additional reproting by Jonathan Allen in New York and Steve Gorman ​in Los Angeles; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Paul Thomasch and Jonathan Spicer)

articles.title: In 2020, Canadian entrepreneur David Ingram bought a rare Aston Martin-designed Hudson Valley home at the rendering stage; six years later, the finished 55-acre compound is listed for $19.5 million
articles.summary: David Ingram, a wellness guru and entrepreneur, has listed his New York residence for $19.5 million, according to a report by Mansion Global.
articles.body: David Ingram, a wellness guru and entrepreneur, has listed his New York residence for $19.5 million, according to a report by Mansion Global. The Toronto-based founder of Sweat and Tonic’s Hudson Valley home is one of only two standalone houses in the world designed by Aston Martin and its partners.Ingram bought the property in 2020, when the house existed only as renderings. He reworked the design, upgrading and expanding the original plans. It took him about five years to build the house. The estate sits in Red Hook, a village in Dutchess County, about two hours from Manhattan and roughly ten minutes from Rhinebeck.A unique home designed by Aston MartinIngram, 60, has been drawn to Aston Martin ever since he saw the classic grey DB5 in the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger. He currently drives a grey DB12, but he still hopes to own an original DB5. This house, therefore, was designed to suit someone who drives an Aston Martin.“It’s the car I’ve always dreamt about and loved the most,” he told the outlet. “Everything about the design and the coolness and association with the brand franchise and its evolution of cars has made the whole thing more fascinating and enjoyable. It’s the kind of house and lifestyle that someone who drives an Aston Martin would live in.”The main residence was designed by Hudson Valley-based S3 Architecture in partnership with Aston Martin’s design studio, Lair. The builders had to work around a rock ledge. This feature helps the home fit into the landscape. A dark metal roof and a façade of blackened cedar keep the building low and understated. The floor-to-ceiling glass brings the beauty of the outdoors inside.A 2,000-foot gated driveway leads to the house, passing old trees, rocky areas and historic stone walls. “The house is spectacular—it’s a piece of art on 55 bucolic acres,” said Jason Karadus of Corcoran Country Living, who listed the house earlier this month, according to the outlet. “It’s one of the highest-priced listings in the history of the Hudson Valley.”Inside the car-themed roomsThe main house spans 7,773 square feet, with four bedrooms, five full bathrooms and two half-baths. The primary suite is cantilevered over the landscape and looks out towards the Catskills. Ingram says that, from the bedroom, you can see past the trees to the mountaintops and the deer that sometimes wander through.“When designing, we always let the land speak first and respond to it. The roofline mimics the jagged edges of the rock ledge reaching down into the earth, as if the home is born of and launching through the landscape,” architecture partner Christopher Dierig said in a statement to the outlet.For the love of cars, the house also has a glass-enclosed automotive gallery underground, with room to display three collector cars. “We wanted the owner and their guests to experience the three-dimensional feel of the house in an organic way, just like you experience one of our cars; there is no single façade that dominates,” said Cathal Loughnane, former head of Aston Martin Partnerships, in a statement.Ingram also agrees that the house never disappoints. “The room I enjoy the most is the one you see as you come around the corner at the end of the drive; it just sticks out so it’s present and so authoritative that you feel like this home was built for that particular vantage point,” he said.Ingram also added an office suite, a cinema, a lounge and a wine storage room to the house.The grounds also offer plenty of room to spread out. A 50-foot pool sits beside the living and dining areas and a fully equipped outdoor kitchen. There is also a tennis court, an architect-designed treehouse, a spring-fed pond, a vegetable garden and trails for walking and ATV riding. Three one-bedroom pods sit down a path, out of sight of the main house. They can serve any purpose, from guest rooms and offices to spaces for homeschooling.Ingram says the decision to sell came down to time. Sweat and Tonic has grown quickly. He has opened three more wellness centres in Toronto and one in West Hollywood, branded Silver Springs, with more planned. As a result, he rarely makes it to the Hudson Valley. Leaving the house empty is a waste of resources. “I’ve really enjoyed every moment of it. I want to give it to someone else brand new while it’s still in perfect condition so they can enjoy it the way I would if I were going to live there,” he told the outlet.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Seth Meyers admits shock over second Trump victory prompted sit-down with late-night team to adjust tone
articles.summary: Seth Meyers revealed he held a tonal meeting with his team after President Donald Trump's second election victory, saying he didn't want to go through the motions again.
articles.body: Late-night host Seth Meyers admitted to shifting his tone after President Donald Trump was elected a second time during an interview on Tuesday and held a meeting about it with his team. Nayeema Raza, host of the "Smart Girl Dumb Questions" podcast, asked Meyers if political comedy makes people feel too comfortable. Meyers said it was a concern but that he didn't know how else to approach it. He also said he didn't want to sound the alarm about the Trump administration every night on his show. "We did have this like tonal conversation at our show, because again, we did not, I mean, twice now, we have been shocked that he has been elected, right? First time more than second, but the second time we sat down with everybody," he said. "I'm like, 'Look, I don't think we can tonally be the same that we were for the first four years, right? I think it's going to be different, and it's going to feel different, and it will also — it will feel like, I don't know, just a little like neutered if we're like going through the motions again,'" Meyers continued. TRUMP IS 'UNFETTERED' AND MORE COMFORTABLE WITH POWER IN HIS SECOND TERM, JOURNALISTS SAY "And so what we do and like what I go out and tell the audience before the show every night is like, 'Look, this show is joyful to do. This is joyful to have you here. And like there's a real strength and joy.' Like, so what we're talking about isn't joyous, but like we — I don't want to perform with like the weight of it all on top of me," he said. "I want to be like honest about it," Meyers added. "We want to get our facts right. But we think there's a strength in, like, sort of being joyful about the fact that we're all together agreeing how f---ing crazy this is." The late-night host also addressed Jimmy Kimmel's suspension during the interview. Kimmel, host of ABC's "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" was suspended in 2025 after comments he made about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. "With that said, like if, like, they turn the lights off fast, when they turn it off, right? Like when Kimmel went off the air, like I don't think he knew that morning that he would be off the air that night. And that was certainly the scariest time of all of this," he said. "The scariest thing about the second term is, like, I feel like there's a lot more going back to the drawing board when you don't get it your first try," Meyers said. Meyers credited NBC News for never telling him what he should "say," and called it a "special thing." BOB IGER BREAKS SILENCE ON DISNEY'S SUSPENSION OF JIMMY KIMMEL OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION COMMENTS "These elitist hosts have spent a lifetime scaring audiences with every move from this administration, so they can insist they're going to lean into joy, but they cannot and will not help themselves," Curtis Houck, managing editor of Newsbusters, told Fox News Digital. "They have this belief that they're like Thomas Paine writing about how 'These are the times that try men's souls,' and any sort of happiness must be seen as a triumph. Cry me a river. Late-night hosts like Meyers have gained increased prominence on the left because of their rabid emphasis on everything Trump and a hyperbolic outlook," he added. Meyers, along with fellow late-night comedian John Oliver, recently joined Kimmel on his show, where the pair described Kimmel as a "bulletproof vest" when it came to Trump. DISNEY CHIEF DANA WALDEN DODGES WHEN ASKED ABOUT JIMMY KIMMEL'S FUTURE AS ABC'S LATE-NIGHT HOST Oliver said that Kimmel comes up a lot during the question-and-answer sessions at stand-up shows he performs with Meyers. "Because they’ll normally say, like, how does it feel being, you know, disliked by the current president? And we always say as long as you’re on the air, we’re fine," Oliver said. "You draw all the ire," Meyers said. "We are fully supportive," Oliver told Kimmel. "We are fully behind you the way that we’re fully behind a bulletproof vest." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The group went on to speculate about why Kimmel drew the most attention from the president, and Meyers said, "Other than the fact that you don't like him, we think he would want to hang out with you."

articles.title: An Indiana father and daughter bought badly eroded farmland with poor corn yields; their soil-restoration efforts are now helping protect a rare salamander
articles.summary: An Indiana father and daughter faced a difficult challenge after buying farmland damaged by years of intensive crop production.
articles.body: An Indiana father and daughter faced a difficult challenge after buying farmland damaged by years of intensive crop production. Deep erosion channels cut through the fields, the soil had lost much of its productivity and corn yields were poor. Ben and Lily Shireman of southern Indiana decided to change how they managed the land, shifting towards rotational grazing, cover crops and other soil-restoration practices. Their efforts have helped reduce erosion, improve pasture conditions and lower the farm's reliance on commercial fertiliser. The work also has wider environmental significance because the property lies within the Blue River watershed, where sediment and agricultural runoff can affect aquatic habitats. The watershed supports the eastern hellbender, a large salamander that depends on clean water and rocky streambeds.How years of farming left the land badly erodedThe Shiremans purchased the farm in Harrison County, southern Indiana, after years of intensive row cropping had damaged its soil. Deep erosion channels cut through the fields, and the family struggled with poor corn yields and high input costs. Ben reported that some of the ditches were so deep that a pickup truck could fit inside them. The farm produced an average of around 100 bushels of corn per acre, and he said the operation was barely making money.How rotational grazing and cover crops helped restore the farmThe family introduced rotational grazing, cover crops and improved pasture management to reduce erosion and rebuild soil health. They also used bale grazing, placing hay bales in selected areas so cattle could feed while distributing manure across the pasture. These practices help return nutrients to the soil and build organic matter. With improved nutrient management, the family reported using less commercial fertiliser. The changes were supported through conservation programmes administered by the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS).Why the farm's soil restoration matters to a rare salamanderThe property lies within the Blue River watershed, where sediment and nutrients from agricultural land can affect waterways. The eastern hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis) depends on clean, flowing water and rocky streambeds for shelter and reproduction. Excess sediment can cover the spaces it needs, while pollution can degrade its habitat. By reducing soil erosion and managing nutrients more carefully, the Shiremans are helping limit runoff into the wider watershed. Their work forms part of the Farmers Helping Hellbenders conservation initiative, which encourages agricultural practices that improve water quality and aquatic habitat.Quail return as the farm's habitat improvesThe family has reported seeing quail return to the property as they improve its soil and pasture conditions. Lily Shireman described the sightings as an encouraging sign of change. Healthier vegetation and better habitat conditions can support wildlife, although the family has not reported a formal survey measuring quail numbers on the farm. For the Shiremans, the changes represent more than an attempt to improve agricultural productivity. They are also helping create a landscape that can support wildlife alongside farming.Conservation assistance helped make the changes possibleThe family received support through the NRCS Environmental Quality Incentives Program and the Farmers Helping Hellbenders Regional Conservation Partnership Program. These initiatives help farmers adopt practices that improve soil health, reduce erosion and protect water quality. The assistance supported changes such as fencing, livestock watering infrastructure and improved grazing management. By tackling soil loss and nutrient runoff at their source, the Shiremans are contributing to wider efforts to protect the Blue River watershed and the eastern hellbender's habitat.You use AI every day. articles.title: Swinney insists 'stars are aligning' for Scottish independence
articles.summary: The first minister will tell delegates at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in Scotland's "journey to nationhood".
articles.body:
John Swinney will insist that "the stars are aligning" for Scottish independence during his keynote speech to the SNP conference later.

The first minister will tell party members in Aberdeen that 2026 has been a turning point in the country's "journey towards statehood".

Swinney will stress that "in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast, every first minister now supports our nations' right to self-determination".

He will seek to press the case for another independence referendum in the wake of elections in May which saw the SNP win a record fifth term in government at Holyrood.

Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'

Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say

'Bring it on': Flynn challenges Burnham on independence referendum

The nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff last month where they signed an agreement , which is not legally binding, that said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

Swinney will tell his party's supporters that "one by one, the stars are aligning in our favour".

He will say that if the SNP lost May's Scottish Parliament election, the case for independence "would have been set back decades".

While the SNP won the Holyrood ballot, the party failed to win the overall majority Swinney had set as a target for trying to force a second referendum in the face of Westminster opposition.

Despite that, Swinney will declare that "there is no turning back".

He is expected to say: "The SNP is making the weather.

"And make no mistake – the wind is now firmly in the sails of Scotland's independence movement."

The first minister will go on to claim that the unionist parties at Westminster are "weaker than they have ever been".

Swinney's address to the SNP conference comes the day after Andy Burnham made his first major speech in Scotland since moving into Downing Street.

The prime minister used that visit to extend an olive branch to Swinney, saying he wanted to work together on giving more power to local communities.

articles.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
articles.summary: For 15 months, a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, accused of ordering the abduction of her children.
articles.body:
It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.

There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.

In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.

There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.

They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.

The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.

On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.

Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.

Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.

All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.

The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.

Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.

In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.

In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.

He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.

She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.

She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.

Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."

The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.

Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.

Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".

Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.

The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

articles.title: Zam-2.0: North Korea tests high-speed AI-guided torpedo; what we know
articles.summary: North Korea has tested a new artificial intelligence-equipped torpedo designed to detect and guide itself towards targets, as Pyongyang steps up efforts
articles.body: North Korea has tested a new artificial intelligence-equipped torpedo designed to detect and guide itself towards targets, as Pyongyang steps up efforts to strengthen its naval capabilities and develop weapons that could pose a greater challenge to South Korea and the United States.The high-speed, precision-guided torpedo, identified as the Zam-2.0, was tested underwater on Thursday to verify technological upgrades, North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported on Saturday. The agency described the test as a success, saying it demonstrated improvements in propulsion technology and marked a potentially significant advance in the country's naval development.The test follows North Korea's underwater launches of two types of strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, its first publicly reported underwater missile tests in nearly three years, according to The Washington Post. The latest demonstrations come amid an intensifying arms race on the Korean Peninsula, with both North and South Korea developing advanced weapons systems designed to overcome missile defences.AI technology and five years of torpedo developmentKCNA said artificial intelligence technology had been incorporated into the Zam-2.0's target detection and guidance systems, although it did not provide further technical details about the weapon or explain how the AI functions.The agency said the Thursday test verified the torpedo's upgraded technology, including improvements in propulsion efficiency and the performance of its rocket propulsion system. More than 180 related tests had been conducted over the past five years to develop the underlying technology, it added.North Korean defence officials who oversaw the test described it as a major success that could bring about a "significant change" in the development of the country's navy, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing KCNA.The announcement is the latest in a series of weapons demonstrations by Pyongyang as leader Kim Jong Un prioritises strengthening the country's naval capabilities alongside its established ballistic missile programme.North Korea has also commissioned two 5,000-tonne destroyers, the Choe Hyon and Kang Kon, and is pursuing the development of submarines capable of launching strategic weapons.Submarine tests add to regional security concernsThe torpedo test comes days after North Korea reported launching two types of strategic cruise missiles from an underwater platform in the country's eastern waters on Wednesday. KCNA said those tests were intended to assess the readiness of underwater combat systems and demonstrate the reliability of the country's war deterrent.In its October 15 report, The Washington Post said the missile launches were likely conducted using the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a submarine unveiled in 2023 that Pyongyang claims can launch tactical nuclear weapons. However, outside experts have questioned the vessel's capabilities, and its operational status remains uncertain.South Korea's military reportedly assessed that the two missiles were launched from a submarine using different launch mechanisms. Analysts said the tests could indicate progress towards deploying the vessel, which would complicate efforts to detect and track North Korean weapons launches.Pyongyang has also been developing a nuclear-powered submarine, unveiled under construction in March 2025, although its completion timeline remains unclear.

articles.title: WA schools chief dismisses girls' sports fairness concerns, says athletes' brains aren't fully developed
articles.summary: Washington Superintendent Chris Reykdal dismissed fairness concerns after Camas High girls cross country athletes protested a biological male competitor.
articles.body: With every word, these leaders shed another shred of dignity. The latest to shrink was Washington state Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal. Appearing on the Seattle-based radio show "Jake and Spike," the head of Washington's public school system made some remarks about the boys-in-girls-sports debate that seemed outlandish by even a politician's standards. The issue at hand was Initiative 638, a Nov. 3 ballot measure in Washington that, if passed, would keep biological males out of K-12 sports. Host Jake Skorheim brought up the situation in southern Washington, where members of the Camas High girls cross country team walked off the start line Tuesday in protest of having to run in the same event as a boy. A CROSS COUNTRY RUNNER SWITCHED TO THE GIRLS TEAM MIDSEASON, PARENTS VOICE THEIR DISAPPROVAL AT MEET Answered Reykdal: "Let's face it, this is happening across the country, where we've empowered young people to make important decisions. And 99% of the time, they're good friends and colleagues, and they respect their transgender colleagues. But some don't agree with it, and that's their right to express that." This doesn't sound too objectionable on its face, but there did seem to be a subtle dig at the protesters. Reykdal said that 99% of young athletes are "good friends and colleagues" and that they "respect their transgender colleagues." It's almost as though he's implying the 1% are disrespectful. No. Surely there are some girls out there who are OK with competing against biological boys. The fact that protesters have received backlash from various teammates proves as much. But just because other athletes aren't going public with their disapproval doesn't mean they like it. They just don't want the smoke that comes with being outspoken. WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR' Second — choosing not to compete against a trans athlete does not make one disrespectful toward the trans community. It is simply acknowledging an unmistakable biological advantage and highlighting the unfairness. Reykdal continued: "The much larger issue here is: Can we accommodate 10, 12, 15 kids a year and make them feel included? Or do we have to go through an initiative process where every single girl has to prove, through one of three methods, that she's a girl in order to participate?" The term "inclusivity" has been co-opted to vilify anyone who opposes males in female sports. The truth is that sports at most levels are designed to be exclusive. Only a certain number of athletes make the team, or get to start, or reach the final heat, or get a scholarship. And those "10, 12 or 15 kids" often have great success. Last year, high school trans athletes won girls' state track-and-field championships in Washington, Oregon and California. And at Camas, a biological male went from 76th in a boys JV race to first in a varsity girls meet. Hence Skorheim's next question. "I hear what you're saying, but specifically, I want to ask about this case in Camas. They're racing against somebody who, earlier in the year, was 76th running for the boys cross-country team, who placed second here. Now, those girls had to forfeit because they had no chance of winning." Answered Reykdal: "Well, I raised two kids, and one of them was a daughter in sports. And my take is, you have a choice to make. You're going to compete and do the best you can and embrace your colleagues, or you're going to walk off and make a statement. And that's okay, too." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER I don't want to put words in Reykdal's mouth, but it almost sounds like he's telling these girls to simply compete, do their best and accept the circumstances — regardless of whether those circumstances are fair. But would he say something similar about athletes competing against people on steroids? That they should just embrace their "colleagues." Probably not. Again, this isn't about discrimination or hate — it's about fairness. But Reykdal's answer to the following question is much more egregious. "If your daughter was running against a boy—an athlete who raced as a boy and was 76th, and then had to race against that same athlete on your team—does that seem like a fair situation to you?" asked Skorheim. Answered Reykdal: "I don't see it that way, Jake. I just don't. These are young, developing people whose brains aren't going to fully develop until they're 25." Excuse me? Sorry, kids, we don't owe you fairness because your brains aren't fully developed. And while we're at it, we can shortchange college athletes because, unless they're at BYU, they're all under 25 as well. I've seen people try to dismiss this issue with an arsenal of arguments — that I-638 proponents are bigoted, that trans athletes are rare or that proving one's gender will require "invasive genital inspections" (untrue). But their brains aren't fully developed is a new one. Again, you won't see politicians bluntly say that it's OK to have boys compete against girls. That's a losing argument. So instead, you get mental gymnastics worthy of the all-around gold. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sorry, but with answers like these — you have to wonder whose brains are truly undeveloped.

articles.title: Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
articles.summary: Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
articles.body:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign.

Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions.

“This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”.

Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”.

Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks.

The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported.

The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks.

According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening.

Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms.

The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.

He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.”

His dismissal “would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership”, he added.

Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.

Rama won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the EU, aiming for membership as early as 2028.

articles.title: An Ohio wetland was taken over by invasive reeds in 2000; by 2022, cattails and other wetland plants had become dominant
articles.summary: A wetland in the western Lake Erie region of Ohio offers researchers a long-term record of vegetation changes following restoration.
articles.body: A wetland in the western Lake Erie region of Ohio offers researchers a long-term record of vegetation changes following restoration. In a study titled The Metzger marsh restoration—a vegetation-centric look after 27 years published in the Journal of Great Lakes Research in its April 2024 issue, Douglas A. Wilcox, Kurt P. Kowalski and Alexandra A. Bozimowski examined Metzger Marsh using vegetation records spanning 1994 to 2022. The research traces changes after a dike was built in 1995 to replace a protective barrier beach that had eroded. Water levels were lowered the following year, and the vegetation changed over the years that followed. By 2000, invasive common reed had become dominant, while later management measures reduced its extent. By 2022, cattails and other wetland plants were dominant. The findings document the changing plant communities recorded during the restoration project.Metzger Marsh restoration: why the dike was builtMetzger Marsh is a coastal wetland in the western Lake Erie region of Ohio, near the Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge and the Metzger Marsh State Wildlife Area. The restoration project was designed to recover a 300-hectare wetland that had deteriorated following the loss of its protective barrier beach.In 1995, a dike was constructed to replace the function of the eroded barrier. Unlike a structure that would completely separate the marsh from the lake, it incorporated a water-control mechanism to allow managers to regulate the connection between the two. A passage for fish was incorporated into the structure, with the design intended to limit the movement of large common carp into the marsh. The researchers examined vegetation before, during and after construction. Their analysis used colour-infrared aerial photographs from 1994 to 2010, together with imagery from 2022. They also carried out quantitative sampling of major vegetation types. These records provided a basis for comparing the plant communities at different stages of the restoration.From mudflat vegetation to invasive common reedThe first recorded changes followed a reduction in water levels in 1996. According to the researchers, the drawdown prompted plants to emerge from the soil’s seed bank, including species associated with exposed mudflats. Tree seedlings also appeared. More than half of the marsh was vegetated during this early period and in subsequent years. The study records the water-control structure opening in 1998. By 2000, invasive Phragmites australis, or common reed, had become the marsh’s dominant plant. Its spread marked a substantial change in the vegetation recorded during the project.The study also records that herbicide use and flooding eliminated most of the trees. Management measures subsequently reduced the area occupied by Phragmites. The sequence matters because the vegetation observed during the first years after the dike was built differed from that found later. Mudflat plants and tree seedlings appeared after the drawdown, followed by the spread of invasive common reed. Subsequent management was accompanied by a reduction in the reed’s extent.Cattails and other wetland plants dominate by 2022By 2022, Typha species, commonly called cattails, had become dominant alongside broadleaf arrowhead (Sagittaria latifolia) and softstem bulrush (Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani). These plants formed the dominant vegetation recorded at the end of the study period, in contrast with the prominence of invasive Phragmites around 2000.The authors concluded that the restoration project had increased habitat value for fish and wildlife. They also identified the project as a useful reference for future restoration work involving land managed by different agencies. The research highlights the practical importance of examining ecological changes across many years when evaluating a wetland restoration project.What the long-term record showsThe study draws on records from 1994 to 2022, an elapsed span of 28 years. Its title describes the restoration as a 27-year project, but the available publication details do not specify how that period was calculated. The findings are best understood through the dated observations and the vegetation changes documented over the study period. Rather than establishing a universal pattern for restored wetlands, the Metzger Marsh research documents the course of one project. It records the initial response to lowered water levels, the later dominance of invasive common reed, subsequent management and the prevalence of cattails and other wetland plants by 2022. Together, these observations provide a long-term basis for understanding vegetation change at the site and evaluating restoration management.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The home ministry Friday expanded the pool of enumerators for the Census exercise, making teachers of not just govt schools but also that of aided or unaided private bodies, societies and trusts; and clerks or officials employed not just by central and state govts but also by public sector undertakings, banks etc, eligible for the assignment.Amending Census Rules 1990, the ministry, in a notification issued Friday, expanded the description of staff who can be hired as enumerators for Census 2027, the second phase of which is due to start in five poll-bound states in Nov, followed by the remaining states (barring the snow-bound UT of Ladakh and parts of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and J&K where it is already over) in Feb next year.The description of those who can be hired as enumerators — encapsulated in Rule 3 of the Census Rules — has been revised from “teachers, clerks or any official or any person” to three distinct categories.Among teachers, those employed in any educational institution of govt, local authority, aided or unaided private bodies, societies or trusts will be eligible to be hired as enumerators. Also, clerks or any official of central govt, state govt, local authority or establishment, including PSUs, statutory bodies, banks, companies, institutions, societies and trusts may be assigned the job of census enumerator.This pool will now also include any person that the state govt or Union territory administration may consider suitable for performing the duties as an enumerator.The amended rules — to be called the Census (Amendment) Rules, 2026 — will offer more clarity to what classes of officials and staff may be hired to carry out the job of census enumerators, apart from expanding the talent pool. articles.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
articles.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.
articles.body:
Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.

US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.

Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.

Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.

Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.

"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.

Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.

"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.

Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.

The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.

The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.

At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".

Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".

But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.

But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.

During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.

Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."

In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.

But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".

"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."

Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.

The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".

A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.

But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.

"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

Sometimes you may realise that pressuring yourself to work faster all the time can affect your concentration or quality. Set real time limits. Prioritise the important over the less important. You’ll be able to think more clearly and make fewer avoidable mistakes if you’re working at a more relaxed professional pace. More intensity does not equal production. articles.title: He started farming on just 1 acre as a student; today his California family farm has 28 greenhouses and 500 customers: Meet Juan Perez
articles.summary: Juan Perez did not set out to become a farmer when he enrolled at California State University, Monterey Bay.
articles.body: Juan Perez did not set out to become a farmer when he enrolled at California State University, Monterey Bay. Yet a series of summer internships helped him discover a career that brought together his interest in science, his family’s farming experience and a desire to build something of his own. What began with a single leased acre has grown into J&P Organics, a family-run organic farm in California’s Salinas Valley. Today, the business grows fresh produce on 10 acres and supplies weekly farm boxes to more than 500 local customers.A student turned 1 acre land into a California family farm Perez’s journey into farming began with uncertainty about his future. His father, Pablo, had spent decades working on farms, and Juan had occasionally worked alongside him. However, his father encouraged him either to work with him or pursue higher education and find another career.As the first member of his family to attend university, Juan chose to study at California State University, Monterey Bay. He selected the university partly because it was only a 20-minute drive from his parents’ home in Castroville, allowing him to live on campus while returning home on weekends.Finding the right subject took time. He initially considered liberal studies, business administration and computer science, but none felt like a suitable fit. A science course eventually caught his attention, particularly the opportunity to conduct research outdoors and work on practical projects.According to Juan Perez’s alumni profile published by California State University, the turning point came when a professor encouraged him to apply for a summer internship at an organic farm. At first, the paid opportunity appealed mainly because he needed money for books, clothes and food. He had little idea that it would influence his career so profoundly. Perez launched J&P Organics with his father a year before walking at his university commencement in 2007. He later completed his capstone project in 2009 and earned a bachelor’s degree in environmental science, technology and policy. The idea was straightforward. Juan had gained knowledge of organic farming, while Pablo brought decades of experience in agriculture. Together, they could combine those strengths and create a family business.His father initially had reservations because he was unfamiliar with organic growing methods. Juan explained that the approach avoided pesticides and chemical treatments, and Pablo agreed to give it a try.Their first step was modest. With a $5,000 loan from the California Coastal Rural Development Corporation, the father and son leased 1 acre of land. They gradually added a second and third acre, eventually expanding to six acres before an opportunity arose to purchase a 10-acre farm in Salinas.According to California State University’s account of Perez’s journey, the same organisation helped them buy the property in 2013, turning their growing operation into a more permanent family enterprise.Three internships helped him discover his futureThe first internship introduced Perez to the practical side of organic agriculture. He researched fertilisers, seeds and pest control, while also creating a small information library that other organic growers could use. The work suited him, and he began to see farming as more than a family connection.His professor, Bill Head, then encouraged him to complete a second summer internship at another organic farm. This experience broadened his understanding of the business, introducing him to marketing, farm-box sales and ways to encourage community support for agriculture.A third internship helped him build connections with people in the farming industry and gain confidence in his own abilities. By the end of that placement, Perez felt ready to start a business of his own.How the farm turned into a family-run operation with 28 greenhousesThe Salinas property has developed into a working farm equipped with 28 commercial greenhouses, a packing shed, delivery vans, tractors, a private water well, fruit trees and open fields. These facilities support the daily work of growing, preparing and distributing produce.Despite its expansion, J&P Organics remains a close-knit family business. Juan and Pablo manage daily operations alongside Juan’s brother, Jose, who works as a mechanic. His mother, Florencia, helps with planting, transplanting, harvesting and packing, while his sister, Cristina, manages the taxes. Juan’s wife, Wendy, supports the business by handling calls, messages, customer questions and orders.The California State University profile notes that four families depend on the farm. Rather than employing an outside workforce, the family shares the responsibilities of running the operation.Fresh produce connects the farm with its communityJ&P Organics grows USDA-certified organic fruits, vegetables and flowers. Each week, customers receive an email explaining which produce will be included in their farm boxes. Orders are then delivered to homes or designated collection points.The farm serves more than 500 local customers, offering them a direct connection to the people who grow their food. Perez has explained in his California State University alumni profile that customers appreciate produce picked shortly before delivery. Even soil left on freshly harvested carrots can reassure buyers that their food has come straight from the ground. Customers can also visit the farm for pick-your-own days, allowing them to experience where their food comes from.Perez believes a small farm can make a differenceThe farm operates in the Salinas Valley, a region widely known for its agricultural production and favourable growing conditions. Its mild climate allows crops to be cultivated throughout the year, across winter, spring, summer and autumn.Perez believes that smaller organic farms can contribute to healthier food choices and more responsible care of the land. While the surrounding region includes much larger agricultural operations, he sees his own farm’s contribution in providing local families with fresh vegetables grown without conventional chemical pesticides.Education is another part of that commitment. As reported by California State University, Perez regularly welcomes elementary and secondary school pupils through the Monterey Bay Aquarium’s WATCH programme. He also hosts college student groups, giving them opportunities to learn about farming through direct experience.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Judge throws out indictment of actor Timothy Busfield
articles.summary: The judge in the case said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner".
articles.body:
A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.

The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations.

The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.

The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward.

Actor Timothy Busfield indicted on child sexual contact charges

State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.

"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.

The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.

The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.

Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.

The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.

The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.

In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.

Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.

Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.

articles.title: Bedbugs found in plane's economy seats force major airline to cancel flight
articles.summary: A Qantas passenger described bedbugs crawling on her belongings and blankets on the Boeing 787 Dreamliner that flew from Perth to Rome. A subsequent flight was canceled.
articles.body: An international flight scheduled to travel from Italy to Australia was abruptly canceled last week when a bedbug infestation was discovered in the cabin during an earlier flight, and the airline issued an apology for the incident. The grounding came after passengers on the nearly 17-hour Qantas journey from Perth to Rome reported being bitten by the insects Oct. 9, The Sydney Morning Herald reported. "We sincerely apologize to customers for the cancellation of Saturday’s Rome-to-Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue [was] identified on a small number of economy seats," Qantas Airways Limited told Fox News Digital. MAJOR AIRLINE ABANDONS 3 KEY CITIES AS PASSENGERS FACE SHRINKING FLIGHT CHOICES Passenger Hailey Bagnall told the TV news program "9News Sydney" that bedbugs were "crawling over our belongings, our clothing, our Qantas blankets, and they were even crawling along the window." The aircraft involved in the incident was a Boeing 787 Dreamliner. Other travelers also recounted their experiences to "9News," with one passenger claiming to be "woken by screaming," while another noted that "the bugs just kept coming." As they collected their bags, the passengers discovered the pests were inside their shoes and crawling on their clothing. Bedbugs were "crawling over our belongings, our clothing, our Qantas blankets, and they were even crawling along the window." Travelers first alerted the flight crew about the bedbugs during the initial Sydney-to-Perth leg of the journey, according to "9News." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The airline said that, before departing on the subsequent long-haul leg to Rome, staff took several preventative measures, including deep cleaning the cabin, removing seat coverings and soft furnishings, and cordoning off the impacted seats. Qantas also noted that its aircraft are regularly cleaned to a high standard and undergo a precautionary disinfectant treatment every 50 days. To alleviate the itchy bites, travelers on the flight were provided with antihistamines, though the crew eventually ran out of the medication, The Sydney Morning Herald reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER After the return flight, which had been due to depart from Rome to Perth Oct. 10, was canceled to complete the deep cleaning, affected passengers were provided with hotel accommodations and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Benjamin Hottel, a Georgia-based entomologist with Orkin, previously told Fox News Digital that bedbugs are skilled at "hitchhiking" on personal belongings. Measuring between 1 and 5 millimeters, the insects feed on human blood. Health officials note, however, that while their bites cause itching and swelling, bedbugs are not known to spread disease and are not considered a public health hazard. Hottel noted that travelers can unknowingly carry bedbugs onto planes, into hotels and eventually back home. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hottel recommended inspecting luggage and clothing after trips and placing travel clothes in a dryer on high heat for about 30 to 45 minutes if exposure is suspected. He said that can help eliminate the insects before they spread inside the home. Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.
